tagline: The war cry that started League's Worlds anthem tradition.
headline: Imagine Dragons wrote League's first Worlds anthem, and over a decade later it's still the one fans return to.
summary: Released for free on September 17, 2014 as the anthem of the League of Legends World Championship, Imagine Dragons' "Warriors" was the first song written for a Worlds and started the yearly anthem tradition. The band played it live for about 40,000 fans at Seoul World Cup Stadium, and its animated video was the most-viewed upload on League's YouTube channel until K/DA's POP/STARS passed it in April 2019. Twelve years on it is still the most-watched Worlds anthem video, was reborn as the Season 2020 cinematic, and keeps coming back to the Worlds stage.

story.heading: Fans first, then a band
story.body:
Before *Warriors* existed, Dan Reynolds was simply a League player. He told NME that his brother and manager Mac pointed him to the free-to-play game around 2013, that he found it frustratingly hard at first, and that he and guitarist Wayne Sermon spent months on the old Twisted Treeline map before moving to Summoner's Rift. By his account the band has gone on stage late because a match wasn't finished. Drummer Daniel Platzman plays too; bassist Ben McKee has said he is the one member who doesn't game.

The link to Riot came almost by accident. One of Reynolds' brothers met a Riot employee at church, the studio reached out, and the band visited Riot's offices, where they became friends with co-founders Brandon Beck and Marc Merrill, Thomas Vu and Christian Linke. Reynolds later called them "kindred spirits." Riot asked for a Worlds anthem while the band was in the middle of making its second album, *Smoke + Mirrors*.

story.heading: A war cry, given away for free
story.body:
*Warriors* arrived as a surprise on September 17, 2014. Riot premiered an animated music video on the League of Legends YouTube channel, and the MP3 was a free download from the League website. Riot pitched it as a war cry for everyone from solo-queue grinders to nervous LCS pros, and that double audience runs through the song: ONE Esports has pointed out that its lyrics speak to everyday players and professionals at the same time.

The band wrote it with Josh Mosser and Alex da Kid, who co-produced it. It came out as a single through Kidinakorner/Interscope and later appeared on the deluxe edition of *Smoke + Mirrors*. The video follows a kid from a dark bedroom setup, through losses in cramped LAN rooms, to the lights of a stadium final. ONE Esports later described the song as a reflection of League's grassroots era, when the line between players, pros and personalities was much blurrier than it is today.

story.heading: Seoul, October 19, 2014
story.body:
Worlds 2014 was the first World Championship held in Asia, with groups in Taipei and Singapore and the knockout rounds in South Korea. About 40,000 fans filled Seoul World Cup Stadium for the final. Before Samsung White and Star Horn Royal Club were introduced, Imagine Dragons performed *Warriors* live with a local orchestra. Samsung White won the Summoner's Cup, and the band returned for a special performance at the closing ceremony. The final was watched by 27 million people.

The night meant something to the band as well. Bassist Ben McKee told The Korea Times that Worlds gave Imagine Dragons its first chance to come to Korea and play for fans there. Seven years later Reynolds told NME that playing Worlds was among his favourite memories.

story.heading: Bigger than the Rift
story.body:
*Warriors* quickly reached listeners outside the game. It peaked at No. 2 on Billboard's Bubbling Under Hot 100 and No. 10 on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs, charted across Europe (reaching No. 7 in Sweden), and was certified 2× Multi-Platinum by the RIAA on April 28, 2023. Hollywood used it in the trailer for *The Divergent Series: Insurgent* and in the final trailer for *Wonder Woman*, and The Korea Times reported that it was the official song of the 2015 FIFA Women's World Cup.

For League, that crossover was the point. A song written for an esports final ended up behind blockbuster trailers and a global football tournament, which took a League anthem far beyond gaming audiences.

story.heading: King of the channel
story.body:
For years the *Warriors* video was the most-watched upload on the League of Legends YouTube channel. In April 2019, K/DA's *POP/STARS* finally passed it, 215 million views to 214 million. *Warriors* kept climbing anyway. It now has about 457 million views, second only to *POP/STARS* on the channel, and it is still the most-viewed Worlds anthem video there, ahead of 2018's *RISE*.

Fans have a ritual around it too. ONE Esports quoted a reader's observation that the video gains new views every time Riot releases a new Worlds song, and its writer admitted to doing the same. Critics keep putting it on top: ONE Esports ranked it the best Worlds song in 2024 and Esports Insider ranked it No. 1 in 2025. Dot Esports, which placed it sixth in 2024, noted that it was still the only Worlds song with a guitar solo.

story.heading: We are warriors: the 2020 rebirth
story.body:
In 2020 Riot did something it had never done with a Worlds anthem: it turned *Warriors* into a season-opening cinematic. *Warriors | Season 2020 Cinematic*, released on January 9, 2020, recast the song as a slow, choral and brooding cover. German composer team 2WEI produced it, Edda Hayes sang it, and the video was made in partnership with Blur Studio. Nine champions share the screen across three storylines. In Demacia, Garen, Lux and Galio hold the line against Sylas and his followers. Ezreal and Kai'Sa fight off a swarm of creatures, while Vi and Caitlyn try to stop Urgot from breaking out of his prison.

The cover became a hit in its own right, with about 176 million views. 2WEI has since returned for *The Call* (2022, again with Edda Hayes), *The Brink of Infinity* (2023) and *Still Here* (2024) season cinematics, and Hayes sang *The Call* at the Worlds 2022 finals opening ceremony.

story.heading: The anthem every anthem answers to
story.body:
Every Worlds since 2014 has had its own anthem, and that tradition starts with *Warriors*. Esports Insider argues that Riot's gamble on an original song for its esport changed what people expected from esports music and laid the groundwork for Riot Games Music's later virtual bands and *Arcane*. The friendship with Imagine Dragons kept paying off too. In 2021 the band returned with *Enemy*, the theme of *Arcane*, a series co-created by Christian Linke, one of the Riot friends the band made in 2014. They performed it at the Worlds 2021 Show Open.

Eleven years after Seoul, *Warriors* was back on the Worlds stage when Chrissy Costanza opened the 2025 final with a medley of it, *Legends Never Die* and *Phoenix*.

whyItMatters: It was the first song written for a League of Legends World Championship and started the yearly Worlds anthem tradition.
It showed that a major-label rock band would write original music for an esport, a bet Esports Insider credits with paving the way for Riot Games Music's virtual bands and Arcane.
Its video was the most-viewed upload on League's YouTube channel until April 2019 and is still the most-watched Worlds anthem video there (about 457M views, second only to POP/STARS on the channel).
It reached the mainstream: 2× Multi-Platinum in the US, Hollywood trailers (Insurgent, Wonder Woman) and the official song of the 2015 FIFA Women's World Cup.
It is the only Worlds anthem Riot has rebuilt into a season-opening cinematic (Season 2020, with 2WEI and Edda Hayes), and more 2WEI season cinematics followed.
The Riot–Imagine Dragons friendship behind it later produced Enemy, the theme of Arcane.

communityMoments.title: A surprise drop, free for everyone
communityMoments.description: Riot premiered the animated video and made the MP3 a free download from the League website, a day before the Worlds 2014 group stage began in Taipei.

communityMoments.title: Live at Seoul World Cup Stadium
communityMoments.description: The band performed Warriors with a local orchestra in the opening ceremony of the Samsung White vs. Star Horn Royal Club final, in front of about 40,000 fans.

communityMoments.title: A closing-ceremony concert
communityMoments.description: Imagine Dragons returned for a special performance at the closing ceremony of Worlds 2014. LoL Esports' official upload marks it as starting at 15:10.

communityMoments.title: Bjergsen coaches the drummer
communityMoments.description: The band's League fandom outlived the anthem: TSM mid laner Bjergsen gave Imagine Dragons drummer Daniel Platzman a Varus coaching session on the official League channel.

communityMoments.title: POP/STARS finally takes the crown
communityMoments.description: After years as the most-viewed video on the League of Legends channel, Warriors was passed by K/DA's POP/STARS, 215 million views to 214 million.

communityMoments.title: We are warriors: Season 2020 begins
communityMoments.description: Riot opened Season 2020 with a choral reimagining by 2WEI and Edda Hayes and a nine-champion cinematic made with Blur Studio. It was the first time a past Worlds anthem had been brought back this way.

communityMoments.title: Imagine Dragons return to Worlds
communityMoments.description: Seven years after Seoul, the band was back at Worlds, performing Enemy, the Arcane theme, with JID at the Worlds 2021 Show Open.

communityMoments.title: The yearly pilgrimage
communityMoments.description: Whenever Riot unveils a new Worlds anthem, fans head back to Warriors to compare. ONE Esports quoted a reader who noticed the old video picks up new views each time.

communityMoments.title: Back on the Worlds stage in 2025
communityMoments.description: Chrissy Costanza opened the Worlds 2025 final in Chengdu with a medley of Legends Never Die, Warriors and Phoenix.

keyMoments.label: Verse 1: the bedroom grinder
keyMoments.description: A power button glows in the dark and a PC fan spins up, the start of the video's journey from nobody to finalist.

keyMoments.label: First chorus
keyMoments.description: The chorus lands and the screen turns into a blood-red battlefield slashed with glowing blade strikes.

keyMoments.label: Verse 2: the LAN room
keyMoments.description: Teams hunch over rows of PCs under strip lights, the grassroots LAN-era scene that ONE Esports singled out.

keyMoments.label: Second chorus: the crowd appears
keyMoments.description: Silhouetted fans and stage lights hint at the arena the team is fighting toward.

keyMoments.label: Final chorus
keyMoments.description: The camera dives into a swirling world and the players turn into giants leaping across it as the last chorus crashes in.

keyMoments.label: The stadium
keyMoments.description: The Worlds stage appears beneath a packed stadium, the destination the whole video has been building toward.

keyMoments.label: The Summoner's Cup
keyMoments.description: The Summoner's Cup appears in a beam of light, the trophy the anthem's warriors are fighting for, before a last close-up of a player's eye.

keyMoments.label: Demacia marches
keyMoments.description: After an opening shot of a mist-shrouded fortress, Garen marches with Demacia's soldiers as the 2020 reimagining begins.

keyMoments.label: Galio awakens
keyMoments.description: The colossus Galio rises out of the dust to shield Demacia's line from Sylas.

keyMoments.label: Lux's last stand
keyMoments.description: Lux rises in front of Galio and the Demacian line for the cinematic's final shot before the logo.

keyMoments.label: Imagine Dragons live at the 2014 final
keyMoments.description: Dan Reynolds and the band perform on the Worlds stage at Seoul World Cup Stadium, just before the finalists are introduced.

keyMoments.label: Closing-ceremony concert
keyMoments.description: Imagine Dragons' closing-ceremony performance begins (15:10, per the official upload).

featuredClip.description: Final chorus: the camera plunges into a swirling world and the players leap across it like giants as streaks of blue light fly between them.
